articles.title: How AI is Accelerating PCB Design and Prototyping - EE Times
articles.text:
The shift from human-driven layout to algorithm-assisted design is reshaping how engineers approach PCB design and prototype services. Instead of requiring weeks of manual layout work, AI tools analyze thousands of potential configurations in minutes, helping engineers identify any issues earlier in the prototyping phase.
For electronics teams evaluating custom PCB prototyping options, these AI-assisted workflows highlight key performance advantages: faster iteration, stronger routing discipline, and tighter handoffs from engineering to production.
Redefining design cycles with AI automation
Designers must make thousands of individual decisions about component positioning, trace routing, and layer allocation. In some workflows, automated tools can reduce tasks that previously took days or weeks to a much shorter period. These tools can also help engineers evaluate design integrity and electrical performance during development.
Quilter claimed that its physics-driven AI has demonstrated this transformation through one of its recent projects. A single engineer used Quilter’s platform to design a functioning two-board computer system in under a week. The project required 38.5 hours of human input, compared to traditional estimates of 428 hours. The company said the baseboard alone showed “12 hours on the baseboard against a 238-hour manual quote,” while the system-on-module required 26.5 hours instead of a conventional estimate of 190 hours.
Efficiency gains like these can enable organizations to test multiple design approaches before committing to production runs, potentially identifying issues earlier and reducing the risk of expensive respins after manufacturing. As a result, engineering resources can focus on novel technical challenges rather than tedious placement and routing tasks.
Optimizing the custom PCB prototype
AI-powered platforms can support prototyping by analyzing patterns from previous projects and presenting engineers with potential design options. The algorithms can draw on vast repositories of design data accumulated from completed boards, identifying successful strategies without requiring explicit programming for every scenario.
According to EMSG, “AI-powered design assistants can suggest optimal component placements, routing paths, and layer configurations.” Engineers designing a custom PCB prototype can leverage platforms that use historical data and machine learning to generate recommendations based on approaches that have performed well in previous designs.
Instead of replacing human expertise, the technology provides informed suggestions that professionals can accept, modify, or reject based on project-specific requirements and architectural constraints.
Real-time assistance during active development helps designers explore creative solutions while maintaining technical rigor. Automated analysis handles repetitive evaluation tasks so professionals can focus on innovation and strategic decision-making. The technology accelerates development cycles while leaving final engineering decisions and validation to the design team.
Accelerating component placement
Positioning hundreds or thousands of components represents one of the most computationally intensive challenges in board development, directly impacting signal integrity, thermal management, and manufacturing feasibility.
Conventional approaches rely on experience-based heuristics that work well for simple layouts but struggle with dense designs containing multiple functional blocks and strict electrical requirements. AI algorithms address these limitations by evaluating vast solution spaces against multiple constraints, allowing engineers to explore options that would be difficult to assess manually within the same timeframe.
Cadence claimed that its Allegro X AI technology has demonstrated the practical impact of this capability. According to Saugat Sen, VP of product marketing at Cadence, one undisclosed customer had a design that “took three days to do PCB placements using manual human methods, but only 75 minutes” when routed through the platform. This not only reduced processing time for complex boards but also included a 14% improvement in wire length.
Shorter connections can support signal integrity and may reduce routing complexity and manufacturing costs. However, the effects on EMI and manufacturing cost depend on the board’s stackup, materials, power requirements, and production process.
Professionals can now conduct early-phase feasibility analysis by quickly testing multiple configurations. Rather than committing to a single approach based on limited assumptions, teams can compare several configurations before investing significant time in detailed routing work.
Solving complex routing and manufacturing challenges
Circuit boards function like cities with multilevel road systems, where hundreds of connection points require careful planning. Bridging upper and lower layers requires vias, which are plated holes that create electrical connections between layers so signals and power can move through the board stack. However, each via introduces unwanted electrical interference while increasing manufacturing complexity and cost. This creates a significant optimization challenge for designers working with dense, high-performance layouts.
InstaDeep said its DeepPCB platform approaches this problem by using algorithms to evaluate and refine routing options. When tested on a benchmark board containing 444 airwires and 157 nets, the company said the system has demonstrated substantial improvements over successive development cycles.
According to DeepPCB, the platform “achieved a remarkable reduction of over 50% in via count” over the past year, producing more efficient configurations by identifying routing paths that conventional planning methods might overlook during manual layout sessions.
Reducing unnecessary vias can simplify fabrication and may improve some electrical characteristics. However, manufacturing yield and reliability depend on the full board design, material selection, fabrication tolerances, and inspection process.
As designs contain fewer potential points of failure, manufacturing yields improve while streamlined layouts accelerate production timelines. By applying lessons from completed projects, the technology helps engineers refine strategies to tackle increasingly complex routing scenarios more consistently.
The future of hardware engineering
Automated routing and placement tools can reduce bottlenecks that once constrained development timelines, allowing professionals to focus on innovation and rigorous testing rather than repetitive tasks. Organizations developing a custom PCB prototype can now allocate more resources toward perfecting functionality before committing to production tooling.
AI-assisted placement and routing are unlikely to eliminate the need for experienced PCB designers. Their more immediate value is reducing the time required to evaluate alternatives, allowing engineering teams to test more configurations before committing to fabrication. The next challenge will be proving that these faster workflows consistently produce designs that meet electrical, thermal, and manufacturing requirements.

articles.title: SA’s HisWay Labs secures funding to help rebuild rail reliability - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
The Cape Town-based HisWay Labs, the company behind TrackView rail-integrity monitoring system, has secured funding from technology investment and product development firm Octoco Group as it prepares for international expansion.
Founded in 2018, HisWay Labs designed TrackView from the ground up for an environment where conventional rail equipment simply doesn’t survive. The solar-powered sensor contains no copper cabling and no batteries, the two components that make traditional trackside infrastructure a prime target for theft.
It is engineered to withstand extreme heat, dust, flooding and deliberate tampering, and to keep monitoring rail integrity and train positioning around the clock without the maintenance burden that legacy systems demand.
Built for the realities of South Africa’s rail network, it is now drawing international attention, and HisWay Labs has taken on strategic investment from Octoco Group to help it prepare for expansion.
TrackView has already earned formal certification and product type approval from the Passenger Rail Agency of South Africa (PRASA) and has been deployed commercially in partnership with Siemens Mobility. The technology is now in active field trials in the United States, and HisWay Labs is exhibiting this month at InnoTrans in Germany, the world’s largest transport technology trade fair, to build European distribution and operator partnerships.
“South Africa has a long tradition of solving hard engineering problems out of necessity,” said Heinrich de Lange, Octoco Group’s MD. “HisWay Labs has turned one of our most damaging infrastructure challenges into a globally competitive product. Backing them is a chance to help restore confidence in our own rail network while proving that world-class industrial hardware can come from here.”

articles.title: AI startup Sol raises $4 million from General Catalyst, Kunal Shah and others
articles.text:
AI startup Sol raises $4M from General Catalyst, Kunal Shah and others
The AI platform of Sol proactively handles email and the funding will be used for R&D & go-to-market initiatives
Artificial intelligence (AI) startup Sol, founded by former executives of Cred, has raised $4 million in funding from General Catalyst, Nexus Venture Partners, DeVC, Peercheque and Kunal Shah.
Sol will primarily use this funding for R&D and go to market initiatives.
Founded in August 2025 by Anish Karan, Prateek Srivastava and Ranjith Nair, Sol primarily automates the whole process of e-mail management where the work can include researching, creating documents, building slides, scheduling time and drafting replies.
The startup further claimed that its tech platform is not limited to drafting replies as once it identifies a commitment and its context, it can create the supporting work the commitment calls for: documents, presentations, research and meeting coordination. The product is designed for the difference between an unanswered email and a finished outcome, it noted.
Though, it added that the user retains the final approval.
“People whose work runs through email often have to repeat themselves: first in email, then again when they ask an AI tool to act. There’s no good reason for that. AI should learn how to use the right tools and skills behind the scenes, so people can focus on the work they’re uniquely good at while Sol does the heavy lifting and gives them a simple way to approve or edit the work,” said Sol CEO Anish Karan.
Sol said its tech platform is designed for people whose work runs through high volumes of email, including founders, executives and professionals in sales, marketing, consulting, recruiting, and agencies.
The company says it operates in its own computer environment where the user can use a browser and draws on a growing library of more than 100 specialist skills. This is initially available through selective access and a waitlist with plans to extend general access soon.

articles.title: Hasta ahora, comprar el Snapdragon más potente era sencillo. Qualcomm acaba de cambiar las reglas con dos nuevos 8 Elite
articles.text:
Hasta ahora, cuando mirábamos la ficha técnica de un móvil Android de gama alta, había una referencia bastante fácil de identificar: el Snapdragon más ambicioso de Qualcomm era también el nombre que señalaba el techo de su catálogo. Eso es justamente lo que ocurría con el Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, la referencia de la generación anterior. Esa lectura acaba de complicarse. La compañía ha presentado dos plataformas de máximo nivel para esta generación. Las dos pertenecen a la misma familia y están pensadas para móviles premium, pero ya no ocupan exactamente el mismo escalón.
En la ficha técnica de un teléfono, el procesador viene decidido por el fabricante y forma parte del conjunto que acabamos comprando. Por eso importa entender cómo Qualcomm ha ordenado esta generación. En la parte superior sitúa al Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, al que describe como su plataforma móvil más potente, mientras que el Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 también está fabricado en 2 nm y busca llevar muchas de esas capacidades a una gama más amplia de móviles de gama alta.
Ficha técnica de los nuevos Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
|  | SNAPDRAGON 8 ELITE EXTREME GEN 6 | SNAPDRAGON 8 ELITE GEN 6 | 
|---|---|---|
| PROCESO DE FABRICACIÓN | 2 nm | 2 nm | 
| CPU | Qualcomm Oryon 2 Prime hasta 5 GHz 6 Performance hasta 4 GHz | Qualcomm Oryon 2 Prime hasta 5 GHz 6 Performance hasta 4 GHz | 
| RENDIMIENTO FRENTE AL 8 ELITE GEN 5 | CPU +13% GPU +44% NPU +35% | CPU +10% GPU +35% NPU +14% | 
| GPU | Adreno Adreno Neural Fusion 18 MB de Adreno High-Performance Memory | Adreno Arquitectura Adreno High-Performance Memory | 
| VÍDEO | 8K a 60 fps Cámara lenta 4K a 240 fps APV | 8K a 30 fps Cámara lenta 4K a 120 fps | 
| CONECTIVIDAD | Qualcomm X105 5G FastConnect 8800 | Qualcomm X105 5G FastConnect 8800 | 
Dos Snapdragon 8 Elite, pero no son iguales
La primera sorpresa aparece al poner las dos fichas técnicas una junto a otra: buena parte de los cimientos son iguales. Tanto el Extreme como el Gen 6 cuentan con CPU Oryon de ocho núcleos, encabezada por dos Prime de hasta 5 GHz, y recurren al mismo X105 5G y a FastConnect 8800 para Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, UWB y Thread. Ambos incorporan además la NPU Hexagon y un amplio conjunto común de capacidades de IA y conectividad.
La distancia empieza a verse cuando pasamos de esa arquitectura común a las cifras de rendimiento que publica Qualcomm. Frente al Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, la compañía atribuye al Extreme mejoras del 13% en CPU, 44% en GPU y 35% en NPU; en el 8 Elite Gen 6, los avances declarados son del 10%, 35% y 14%, respectivamente. Conviene recordar que estamos ante cifras reveladas por la propia Qualcomm y que resultados pueden variar según la implementación de cada fabricante de móviles.
Otro de los pilares de esta generación es la IA. Los dos procesadores combinan la NPU Hexagon, el Sensing Hub y la CPU Oryon para ejecutar en el dispositivo funciones capaces de utilizar contexto personal, aprender de hábitos y coordinar tareas entre aplicaciones con menos intervención del usuario. Qualcomm también plantea usos de IA generativa como resumir documentos, redactar respuestas o generar imágenes y vídeo. En el Extreme lleva esta apuesta más lejos y destaca soporte para modelos Mixture of Experts de más de 30.000 millones de parámetros.
Las diferencias se vuelven todavía más concretas en gráficos y vídeo. En el Extreme, Qualcomm incorpora Adreno Neural Fusion y especifica 18 MB de Adreno High-Performance Memory, mientras que en cámara eleva la grabación hasta 8K a 60 fps y la cámara lenta 4K hasta 240 fps, además de incorporar soporte para el códec APV. En el 8 Elite Gen 6, el techo oficial se queda en 8K a 30 fps y cámara lenta 4K a 120 fps. Ahí es donde la separación entre ambos deja de ser únicamente una cuestión de porcentajes y empieza a traducirse en capacidades específicas.
¿Qué significa todo esto cuando llega el momento de elegir móvil? El Extreme queda como la opción con la que Qualcomm pretende llevar más lejos el rendimiento, los gráficos, la IA y la creación de contenido, mientras que el 8 Elite Gen 6 conserva buena parte de esa base y busca extenderla a un abanico más amplio de teléfonos premium. Eso no permite concluir, por sí solo, que cualquier móvil con el Extreme vaya a ser mejor en términos absolutos: la propia compañía advierte de que los resultados dependen de cómo implemente la plataforma cada fabricante.
Qualcomm ha confirmado que esta nueva familia llegará a móviles de Honor, iQOO, Motorola, Nubia, OnePlus, OPPO, REDMI, RedMagic, vivo, Xiaomi y ZTE, aunque no detalla en esta nota qué plataforma utilizará cada modelo concreto. Esa será la consecuencia práctica de esta generación: dos Snapdragon 8 Elite convivirán en la parte alta del mercado y obligarán a leer las especificaciones con algo más de atención.

articles.title: OPPO Find X10 Pro Max: Price, release date, specs, and features
articles.text:
OPPO launched the Find X10 Pro Max in China on September 22, 2026, making it the first Pro Max model in the Find series and the world’s first smartphone with three 200MP rear cameras.
The phone starts at CNY 6,799 (about $1,006) in China, with sales beginning September 24. OPPO has confirmed that the Find X10 Pro Max will launch in international markets, but it has yet to announce a global or Nigerian release date and price.
This guide covers the Find X10 Pro Max’s price, specifications, cameras, features, and what to know before buying it in Nigeria.
Dollar prices in this article are rough conversions at CNY 6.7074 to $1 on September 23, 2026. They are not official US or African prices.
What is the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max?
The Find X10 Pro Max is the top phone in OPPO’s new Find X10 lineup, sitting above the Find X10 and the Find X10 E. OPPO skipped a Find X10 Pro this year.
Its biggest selling point is the camera: the Pro Max uses a 200MP ultrawide camera, while the regular Find X10 uses a 50MP one. Both phones share a 200MP main camera and a 200MP telephoto camera.
The phone arrives soon after the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the vivo X500 Pro Max. OPPO wants to win you over with photos, and it gives you several strong lenses so you can shoot almost any scene.
OPPO Find X10 Pro Max release date
Here is where the launch stands today:
- China launch: September 22, 2026
- China sales: September 24, 2026, from 10 a.m. local time
- Global launch: confirmed, but OPPO has not named a date
- Nigeria and other African markets: no date yet
OPPO announced the Find X10 Pro Max’s chip and confirmed plans for a global launch event on September 15. Some specification sites list September 15 as the phone’s global release date, but that is the announcement date, not the start of sales. OPPO has not yet announced when the phone will go on sale globally.
OPPO launched the Find X9 and Find X9 Pro internationally in 2025, and the Find X9 Ultra also received a global launch in 2026. However, availability varies by market, so that history does not guarantee a Nigerian release for the Find X10 Pro Max.
For now, wait for OPPO to confirm the launch date, price, and availability in Nigeria before making plans to buy the phone.
OPPO Find X10 Pro Max price
OPPO announced four versions in China:
| RAM and storage | China price | About (USD) | 
|---|---|---|
| 12GB + 256GB | CNY 6,799 | $1,014 | 
| 12GB + 512GB | CNY 7,499 | $1,118 | 
| 16GB + 512GB | CNY 7,999 | $1,193 | 
| 16GB + 1TB | CNY 8,999 | $1,342 | 
The Hasselblad Teleconverter Kit costs CNY 1,099 (about $164) in China. You buy it separately from the phone.
Expected price in Nigeria
OPPO has not announced a Nigerian price yet. A straight conversion of the China prices gives you a rough guide:
- At the official rate of ₦1,327.78 to $1 on September 23 (as reported by Vanguard), the phone works out to about ₦1.35 million to ₦1.78 million.
- At the parallel market rate of about ₦1,389 to $1, it works out to about ₦1.41 million to ₦1.86 million.
Expect the final price in Nigeria to land higher. Import duties and dealer margins add to the cost, and the naira rate changes often.
You may see early listings on Jumia, Konga, Slot or Jiji before OPPO launches the phone here. Before you pay for one, check:
- The exact model number
- Whether it is a China unit
- What warranty comes with it
- Whether it works on your network, such as MTN or Airtel
Price in other African markets
OPPO has not announced official prices for the Find X10 Pro Max in South Africa, Kenya, or Ghana. Until local pricing is confirmed, the China prices above give you a sense of where the phone sits in OPPO’s lineup, but they should not be treated as estimates for African markets.
If you’re planning to buy the phone, wait for OPPO to announce the price in your country before setting your budget.
OPPO Find X10 Pro Max specs at a glance
| Feature | China model | 
|---|---|
| Display | 6.78-inch flat screen, 2772 x 1272 | 
| Refresh rate | 1Hz to 120Hz, up to 144Hz in some games | 
| Chip | MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro | 
| Memory and storage | 12GB or 16GB RAM, up to 1TB storage | 
| Rear cameras | Three 200MP cameras plus a colour sensor | 
| Front camera | 50MP with autofocus | 
| Battery | 8,000mAh | 
| Charging | 80W wired and 50W wireless | 
| Software | ColorOS 17 (Android 17) | 
| Protection | IP68 and IP69, plus IP66 | 
These specs come from OPPO’s China website. Some features and accessories may change when the phone reaches other markets.
Detailed specs
1. Display
The Pro Max has a 6.78-inch flat screen with a 2772 x 1272 resolution. The screen changes speed from 1Hz to 120Hz as you use it. In some games, it goes up to 144Hz.
OPPO says the screen reaches up to 2,000 nits across the full display, so you can read it in bright sun. It also uses 3,840Hz PWM dimming, which is easier on your eyes at night.
2. Performance and storage
MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro powers the phone. The chip uses a 2nm process. OPPO pairs it with 12GB or 16GB of LPDDR5X RAM and up to 1TB of UFS 4.1 storage.
Pick your storage size with care, since the phone has no memory card slot. OPPO says the chip delivers 17% better overall CPU performance than the last generation. Reviews will show how it holds up in daily use.
3. Rear cameras and video
The Pro Max has four cameras on the back:
- Main: 200MP, 24mm, f/1.5, with optical image stabilisation (OIS)
- Ultrawide: 200MP, 13mm, f/2.2, with a 124-degree view
- Telephoto: 200MP, 70mm, f/2.1, with OIS, 3x optical zoom and close-up shots from 10cm
- Colour sensor: helps the phone get colours right
OPPO says the main camera captures up to 17 stops of dynamic range at 1x. In simple terms, it keeps detail in bright skies and dark shadows in the same photo.
For video, you get 8K at 30fps and 4K at up to 120fps. OPPO also offers 8K Log recording and Open Gate capture for creators. Check which video modes work on each lens once the phone reaches stores.
4. Front camera
The selfie camera is 50MP with autofocus. It records video at up to 4K 60fps.
5. Design and colours
You can pick Moon White or Warm Orange. There is also a Light Titanium version. These are English versions of OPPO’s China colour names.
The Moon White model mixes two finishes on the back, a look OPPO says comes from classic cameras. The phone is about 8.4mm thick and weighs about 233g to 235g, based on the colour. OPPO also adds a physical Snap Key so you can take photos faster.
The phone can handle rough use. It carries IP68 and IP69 ratings for dust and water, plus an IP66 rating. It also has an SGS five-star drop rating. These ratings come from lab tests, so treat them as extra protection and still handle your phone with care.
6. Battery and charging
An 8,000mAh silicon-carbon battery powers the phone. It supports 80W SuperVOOC wired charging and 50W wireless charging.
The China box includes a charger. Check the box contents where you buy it, since packages can differ outside China.
7. Software and connectivity
The phone runs ColorOS 17, based on Android 17. It also comes with:
- An ultrasonic fingerprint sensor under the screen
- Stereo speakers
- Wi-Fi 7 and NFC
- A USB-C port
If you import a China unit, check that it supports your network bands before you pay. The China model number is PMX110.
What does the Hasselblad Teleconverter Kit do?
The kit clips onto the telephoto camera so you can shoot far-away subjects, like a singer on stage or a player on the pitch.
OPPO says the kit gives you 10x optical zoom and 20x lossless zoom. Digital zoom goes up to 200x. The kit also adds a stage preset and 4K 60fps Dolby Vision video. Your results will still depend on the light and the subject.
The kit costs CNY 1,099 and comes with:
- The teleconverter lens
- A matching phone case
- An adapter ring and a hand grip
- A shoulder strap and a storage bag
Without the kit, the phone gives you 3x optical zoom and up to 120x digital zoom.
How the Find X10 Pro Max compares with the rest of the lineup
| Model | China starting price | Chip | Rear cameras | Battery | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Find X10 Pro Max | CNY 6,799 (about $1,014) | Dimensity 9600 Pro | 200MP main, 200MP ultrawide, 200MP telephoto | 8,000mAh | 
| Find X10 | CNY 5,499 (about $820) | Dimensity 9600M | 200MP main, 50MP ultrawide, 200MP telephoto | 8,000mAh | 
| Find X10 E | CNY 4,999 (about $745) | Dimensity 9500s | 50MP main, 50MP ultrawide, 50MP telephoto | 7,025mAh | 
Pick the Pro Max if you want the 200MP ultrawide camera and the top chip. If you want to spend less, the Find X10 keeps two 200MP cameras and the same 8,000mAh battery, while the Find X10 E gives you the lowest price in the series.
Should you wait for the Find X10 Pro Max?
Wait for the Pro Max if you take lots of photos and videos. Waiting also lets you compare the local price and warranty against an imported unit.
If you need a phone now, look at these two OPPO phones:
- Find X9 Pro: a 200MP telephoto camera and a 7,500mAh battery
- Find X9 Ultra: two 200MP cameras and a 10x optical telephoto camera
Compare prices and warranty in your area before you choose.
Frequently asked questions
Q) When will the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max launch globally?
- OPPO confirms a global launch, but it has not shared the date yet. The company says it will share more details at a future global event.
Q) How much will the Find X10 Pro Max cost in Nigeria?
- OPPO has no official Nigerian price yet. The China model starts at CNY 6,799, which is about $1,014 or roughly ₦1.35 million at the official rate. Expect the local price to land higher once duties and dealer margins apply.
Q) Can I buy the China version for use in Nigeria?
- Yes, sellers may offer imported China units. Check the model number (PMX110), network bands, software and warranty before you pay.
Q) Does the Find X10 Pro Max have a Snapdragon chip?
- It uses the MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro chip.
Q) Is there an OPPO Find X10 Pro?
- OPPO skipped the Pro model this year. The Pro Max sits at the top of the lineup, with the Find X10 and Find X10 E below it.

articles.title: Meta Connect 2026: cuándo es, hora y cómo ver en vivo los anuncios de Mark Zuckerberg
articles.text:
Mark Zuckerberg publicó en sus redes sociales un video expectativa sobre el Meta Connect 2026 que será el 23 de septiembre. (Tomado de @zuck)
Meta Connect 2026 comenzará este miércoles 23 de septiembre con una presentación de Mark Zuckerberg, fundador y director ejecutivo de Meta, centrada en inteligencia artificial (IA), gafas inteligentes y realidad virtual.
La conferencia se realizará desde Menlo Park, California, y podrá seguirse sin costo a través de la transmisión oficial de la empresa. El evento llega con anuncios anticipados sobre nuevos dispositivos y funciones de software.
PUBLICIDAD
Entre los posibles lanzamientos aparece una línea de gafas sin cámara, un visor de realidad mixta identificado como Phoenix y novedades sobre Muse, el agente de inteligencia artificial que Meta busca incorporar a sus lentes y servicios.
Cuándo se hará Meta Connect 2026
La conferencia principal de Meta Connect 2026 tendrá lugar el miércoles 23 de septiembre. Zuckerberg será el encargado de abrir el evento, en el que la compañía prevé presentar su hoja de ruta para el desarrollo de hardware, asistentes de IA y experiencias inmersivas.
Meta programó sesiones técnicas para el segundo día, destinadas a desarrolladores y personas interesadas en el ecosistema de aplicaciones de la empresa. Para seguir el discurso principal no será necesario crear una cuenta ni completar un registro previo.
PUBLICIDAD
A qué hora comienza el discurso de Mark Zuckerberg, CEO de Meta
La presentación de Zuckerberg está prevista para las 20:00 de Argentina. En Colombia, el inicio será a las 18:00; en Ciudad de México, a las 17:00; y en España, a la 1:00 del jueves 24 de septiembre, por la diferencia horaria.
La agenda sitúa el comienzo de la conferencia a las 17:00 en California, donde se encuentra la sede de Meta. La empresa anunció que el discurso estará dedicado a las novedades en IA agéntica, dispositivos portátiles y realidad virtual, tres áreas que concentran buena parte de su inversión tecnológica.
Cómo se podrá ver en directo Meta Connect 2026
La conferencia se retransmitirá de forma gratuita en el canal virtual oficial de Meta Connect. El público podrá acceder al video en directo desde el sitio de la compañía, sin necesidad de inscripción para ver la exposición inicial de Zuckerberg.
PUBLICIDAD
Meta habilitó un registro opcional para recibir recordatorios y consultar el programa completo de actividades. Esa inscripción permitirá acceder a las sesiones técnicas del segundo día, que suelen incluir demostraciones, anuncios para desarrolladores y detalles sobre herramientas de software.
Qué novedades presentaría Meta sobre gafas inteligentes
Uno de los anuncios que genera más expectativas es un supuesto modelo de gafas inteligentes sin cámara, conocido internamente como “Luna”, según The Information.
El dispositivo conservaría micrófonos, altavoces y un botón lateral para activar el asistente Meta AI, pero eliminaría el sensor visual presente en las Ray-Ban Meta.
Las gafas sin cámara tendrían dos estilos y sumarían micrófonos adicionales para interactuar con el asistente de IA. La decisión respondería a las críticas por la posibilidad de registrar imágenes de otras personas sin que adviertan que están siendo filmadas.
PUBLICIDAD
Andrew Bosworth, director de tecnología de Meta, adelantó en una sesión de preguntas en Instagram que la empresa tendría más información sobre ese asunto durante Connect.
Asimismo, la compañía podría mostrar una tercera generación de las gafas Ray-Ban Meta, fabricadas junto con la marca de anteojos. Ray-Ban anticipó la llegada de nuevo hardware, aunque todavía no precisó qué producto presentará con Meta.
Cómo Meta innovaría en realidad virtual
Otra posibilidad es la presentación de Phoenix, un visor de realidad mixta que apareció en imágenes filtradas dentro de una actualización de HorizonOS.
A diferencia de los cascos Quest, el dispositivo tendría un formato más delgado, similar a un antifaz, y se conectaría por cable a un módulo externo que concentraría el procesamiento.
PUBLICIDAD
Phoenix prescindiría de controles físicos y usaría seguimiento de manos y ojos, de acuerdo con las versiones conocidas hasta ahora. El dispositivo podría incorporar el procesador Snapdragon Reality Elite de Qualcomm, diseñado para reducir el peso de los visores de realidad mixta.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Exclusive: CoreWeave launches Remote Key Encryption to keep customer keys off its cloud - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Exclusive: CoreWeave launches Remote Key Encryption to keep customer keys off its cloud
Artificial intelligence cloud provider CoreWeave Inc. today unveiled Remote Key Encryption, a service that encrypts customer data sitting on its infrastructure with keys the company itself never holds.
The service takes aim at the key-custody problem that keeps enterprise AI projects parked in security review. Auditors want a named list of everyone able to decrypt sensitive material, and on most clouds the cloud provider is on that list. Model weights and training checkpoints fall under the same rules as any other regulated corporate data, which leaves security teams reconciling an infrastructure choice against obligations written well before the workload existed.
Encryption under the new service runs client-side, inside a customer’s own compute boundary, using keys generated and stored in whatever secrets manager, key management system or hardware security module that customer already operates. No key is imported into a CoreWeave-side key store, so the company holds only ciphertext.
Access to the nodes themselves stays gated behind CoreWeave’s Support Access Management controls. Support engineers at the company cannot reach those nodes without a customer’s express permission, according to the announcement.
Rotation, expiration and revocation run on the customer’s existing schedule and tooling. CoreWeave said the service drives rotation and deletion through that infrastructure rather than standing up a parallel set of controls, and that its approach to key lifecycle management is patent pending. The encryption algorithms underneath are standard ones.
“The fastest path through the loop to production isn’t a new security model,” Andy Manoske, product lead for enterprise and security at CoreWeave, and Paul Friedman, head of security foundations, wrote in a blog post. “It’s making sure our security layer speaks fluently to the one you have already built.”
The same argument drives CoreWeave’s identity work, which landed earlier. CoreWeave IAM handles authentication and authorization across the company’s cloud and federates with enterprise identity providers, Microsoft Corp.’s Entra and Okta Inc. among them, leaving the customer’s own provider as the source of truth. Automated User Provisioning, introduced last November, syncs users and groups continuously, so a hire, a role change or a termination propagates across CoreWeave Kubernetes Service, AI Object Storage and the console without anyone filing a ticket.
Training clusters are a harder case. CoreWeave’s offering for them is SUNK, which packages the open-source job scheduler Slurm for Kubernetes. Slurm keeps a notion of identity all its own, built on POSIX users, groups and accounts, and reconciling those accounts with a corporate directory has traditionally been manual work.
SUNK User Provisioning creates the POSIX user and groups, syncs SSH keys and sets up the Slurm account the moment a federated user turns up in CoreWeave IAM. Add a researcher to a group in Entra or Okta, the company said, and that person can log in to a cluster node inside a minute with the right permissions already set.
Remote Key Encryption enters limited availability later this year, with IBM Corp. as a launch partner. The first release protects data on CoreWeave AI Object Storage using keys held in HashiCorp Vault, HashiCorp Vault Enterprise or any key management or hardware security product supporting the Key Management Interoperability Protocol. IBM acquired HashiCorp Inc. in February 2025.

articles.title: Google's Googlebook isn't a better Chromebook, it's an attempt to rebuild the PC around Android
articles.text:
Looking ahead: Google has completely pulled back the curtain on its replacement for the Chromebook platform, designed to tackle Windows and macOS head-on. The upcoming notebooks from Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo aim to bring the Android software stack to a full-blown PC operating system for Arm and x86 devices.
Pre-orders are now open for the first Googlebook laptops from five manufacturers. Starting prices range from $899 to $1,299.
Google is positioning the notebooks as the ultimate companions for Android phone owners. When a user first signs into a Googlebook, it can instantly import the phone's settings, saved passwords, and Wi-Fi connections.
Similar to how Macs can access all the files and apps on a user's iPhone, a Googlebook can seamlessly summon an Android phone's files and messages. Users can start a task on a mobile app and continue on the Googlebook. The machines combine the Android and Chromebook environments by natively supporting Android apps alongside a desktop-grade Chrome experience, complete with extensions.
Unsurprisingly, Google's AI assistant, Gemini, is at the core of the OS. Wiggling the mouse summons the assistant to answer questions and complete various tasks. A dedicated button, called Rambler, also transcribes spoken words into headers, checklists, formatted takeaways, and other documents. Users can also use prompts to create custom widgets or build apps through the Antigravity AI agent platform.
Each Googlebook includes a year of Google AI Pro and three months of YouTube Premium, Adobe Photoshop, and more. Google promises to provide up to a decade of content and feature updates.
The Dell and HP Googlebooks run on Snapdragon X Elite processors, while Intel Core Ultra 5 chips serve as the baseline for the others, and all of the SoCs include NPUs that achieve up to 45 TOPs. With a 13.4-inch 2.5K LCD touchscreen, Dell's XPS Googlebook is the smallest. The others sport 14-inch 2.8K OLED panels, except Lenovo's, which measures 15.3 inches. Starting models all include 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, and some are upgradeable to 32GB of memory.
Other features include backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, and Google's Glowbar, which displays patterns in response to boot cycles, battery level, and AI actions. Google's Titan C2 security chip supports fingerprint readers on all models, while the HP and Lenovo notebooks also include facial unlock. The laptops also feature aluminum, magnesium alloy, and carbon fiber chassis.
Googlebooks will be available starting October 4 in the US and October 5 in Canada, the UK, Ireland, France, Germany, and Australia.

articles.title: US and China propose hotline to de-escalate AI threats ahead of Washington summit
articles.text:
US and China propose hotline to de-escalate AI threats ahead of Washington summit — comms channel between both nations to be left open in case of national security threats posed by autonomous artificial intelligence
A red telephone for the 21st century.
The U.S. and China have proposed developing a hotline for AI incident reports to address the risk of a rogue AI model getting out of control and to prevent misinterpretations of attacks that could trigger rapid autonomous escalation, Reuters reports. This news comes ahead of a planned visit by Chinese Premier Xi Jinping to Washington on September 24. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also confirmed that follow-up AI safety discussions are scheduled between the two nations in two months' time.
All of this sits against the backdrop of ongoing U.S. China trade and relations talks, in addition to various frontier AI agents seemingly breaking out of their containment and hacking organizations without oversight from humans.
While some are raising the alarm about the humanitarian risk posed by AI models, the U.S. and China are taking steps to ensure that if either party does end up triggering a dangerous AI event, there may be the opportunity for a joint response from both nations ahead of any potential perceived threat or escalation.
As artificial intelligence continues to make headlines circling around safety, both the U.S. and China now appear to be building global safeguards through a dedicated hotline to discuss any AI-related issues that escalate to national security threats.
Keeping humans in the loop
Following discussions between Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York over the weekend, the two sides have proposed that President Trump and Xi Jinping discuss various AI safety mechanisms, including a notification system focused around national security. This could include warnings of detected rogue AI actors operating anywhere in the world, as well as informing the other partner if an autonomous system performed an action that could be misinterpreted as an attack.
The scenario both parties want to avoid is an AI-driven autonomous weapon system — be they kinetic or something more asymmetric in nature, like AI-driven cyber attack capabilities — responding to provocation without consideration by a human. That could then trigger an escalated response in another AI system, leading to rapid escalation to full-blown conflict at a pace where humans wouldn't be able to intervene.
The proposed system could also help both parties develop joint responses to positive goals, as well as potential threats. This could form the basis for joint development pacing, considering the recent calls from U.S. AI firms to slow AI development to improve alignment and safeguards. China is less keen, suggesting that such a move could be used to hamper Chinese AI developments.
It's not clear at this time how keen China is to implement the proposed notification system, but analysts and experts on both sides have called for a system like this to be developed. Both the U.S. and China have agreed to further broach AI safety concerns in the coming months.
Laying the groundwork
We're still in the very early days of these discussions, with only the bare bones of a proposal for a hotline in place, and much to discuss on alignment between the two major AI-developing countries. The next step will be the talks between the two leaders, where much more than AI will be discussed.
If the relationship between the U.S. and China can move beyond its ongoing rivalry, the potential is there for much firmer agreements on the specifics around AI integration in national security and military actions. Although some analysts remain sceptical of firm agreements because of the limited trust between the two parties, there is some hope that agreements can be made on the direct weaponization of AI, core principles of AI safeguarding, and preventing them from targeting or damaging critical infrastructure.
The hope for a successful meeting is very much bipartisan. Leading Democrat in the U.S. House, Representative Ro Khanna, said that the first thing President Trump and Xi Jinping should work on in their meeting is developing core AI principles. Particularly around banning recursive self-improving AI and removing the option to use such autonomous systems on biological and nuclear weapons technology.
Washington's summit between President Trump and Xi Jinping is scheduled to begin in just a few days, where much more will be discussed beyond AI safety, as the rest of the world waits with bated breath, as the meeting between the two leaders could set the stage for another round of discussions surrounding the two nations' economic relations.
Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

articles.title: Silent Hill: Townfall starts incredibly strong but gets maddeningly tedious
articles.text:
Scotland is a place that’s near and dear to my heart. Because my maternal grandparents hail from the country, I’ve travelled there several times and the culture as a whole has been a part of my life here in Canada. While I unfortunately haven’t returned in many years, Silent Hill: Townfall made me feel like I’ve been transported there.
It’s hard to explain. There’s something uniquely special about the country, like a pervasive warm coziness that seeps through its old architecture and rural towns, and Glaswegian developer Screen Burn so vividly captures all of that in Townfall while twisting it on its head. Set in 1996 in the fictional coastal village of St. Amelia (based on the real St. Monans), Townfall follows an American named Simon Ordell (The Leftovers‘ Jovan Adepo) as he washes ashore with no memory, IVs attached to him, and visions of a nurse named Zoe.
Admittedly, the premise of a man pursuing a woman in a mysterious fog-filled town is very similar to the likes of Silent Hill 2, but developer Screen Burn moves beyond the familiar trauma metaphors to explore corporate malfeasance and Thatcherism, particularly with respect to its impact on the healthcare system. The town also gets drenched in an eerie, almost apocalyptic shade of red, which introduces strange metallic pipes that block previously accessible routes and even hint at cosmic horror elements. All of this gives Townfall a unique flavour within the Silent Hill pantheon, even as Simon himself can often be a decidedly muted character.
And the first few hours of the game are truly sublime. Through the series’ first-ever full first-person POV, all of St. Amelia’s little corner shops, pharmaceutical ads and charity boxes feel all the more tactile and lived-in. The sense of haunting atmosphere is palpable here; gone are the typically friendly Scots who would populate these places, a feeling of isolation that’s only enhanced by eerie lighting in the streets and Canadian Pilotpriest’s moody ambient score.
The only others here, naturally, are monsters, represented here in the form of Slender Man-esque creatures that shamble and wail along the streets. And in a refreshing change of pace from last year’s ridiculously action-focused Silent Hill f, Townfall emphasizes stealth, so your best course is to try to steer clear of these fiends. While Simon can use a small assortment of weapons that include wooden planks, steel pipes and a revolver, combat is deliberately sluggish and durability and ammo are markedly minimal to make each encounter feel harrowing.
Instead, you have to use a handheld CRTV to track the ever-changing locations of enemies and attempt to skirt around them with the help of throwable objects and other sources of noises to distract them. This creates a nail-biting sense of tension as you hear a radio crackle to denote a nearby enemy, especially when there are multiple in the vicinity, and you can only monitor one at a time. Sometimes, I’d find myself trying to crouch-walk away from one, only to be discovered by another, frantically running into a nearby convenience store and locking the door for momentary respite. Other instances make smart use of the 90s setting, like an apartment in which I had to print photos in an adjacent room using a slow dial-up computer while an enemy was nearby. Sequences where you don’t have access to the CRTV, naturally, are all the more distressing.
Unfortunately, Townfall ruins this incredibly measured sense of tone and pacing by later throwing in a new recurring enemy type known as The Weight. This hulking brute is practically invincible, can run extremely fast and kills you in one shot, making him feel painfully unfair. What’s more, he’s first introduced in a basement setting in which you have to methodically check one of many rooms for the necessary items to progress, which becomes tedious as he’s constantly hounding you and, sometimes, even blocks your path.
And because these areas are comparatively much more claustrophobic and dimly lit than the streets of St. Amelia, it’s not like you can even easily sneak around him. It often just felt like trial and error of attempting to search one room, dying to him, then repeating with subsequent rooms. This sense of frustration is compounded by the fact that The Weight actively counters the IV drip system, which lets you combine materials to revive yourself upon death. Sometimes, I’d come back to life, only for The Weight to suddenly circle back and kill me again.
If I’m being generous, it would seem like this was an attempt at a stalker-type enemy like Mr. X from Resident Evil, but The Weight is far too nimble, erratic and powerful to evoke the same kind of looming threat. Instead, it’s just overbearing and completely upends the compelling gameplay loop.
Ultimately, Silent Hill: Townfall is worth playing due to its immaculate sense of place and (often) tightly-crafted fear-inducing stealth sequences. Just know that there’s more than a wee bit of a tedious grind in between those highs.
Silent Hill: Townfall launches on PS5 and PC on Sept. 24.

articles.title: Marvel confirma otro personaje que sí recuerda a Peter Parker: nunca habrías imaginado cuál
articles.text:
En el Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel, Peter Parker es un absoluto desconocido para todo el planeta. El personaje de Tom Holland sacrificó su propia identidad en Spider-Man: No Way Home e hizo que, por medio de la magia de Doctor Strange, el mundo entero se olvidase de él. En Spider-Man: Brand New Day descubríamos que Hulk transformado en gigante verde sí lo recordaba. Y ahora, la compañía ha confirmado un personaje más que aún le tiene en su memoria.
Con motivo del estreno de VisionQuest, Marvel está lanzando varios teasers y adelantos para que los fans confíen en el proyecto. Y es precisamente en uno de ellos donde se ha confirmado lo que nadie esperaba. Hay otro personaje de Marvel que recuerda a Peter Parker. Se trata de E.D.I.T.H., la asistente de Inteligencia Artificial que Tony Strak creó para el propio Spider-Man.
En VisionQuest, tanto E.D.I.T.H. como el resto de IAs de la saga tendrán forma humana. Y en un nuevo vistazo detrás de las cámaras, en un breve clip compartido por Entertainment Tonight, se puede ver al propio Visión hablando con ella y explicándole sus problemas para «lidiar con adolescentes». Ante ello, en tono alegre, E.D.I.T.H. le responde: «Qué me vas a contar: mi primer jefe estaba en el instituto». Por supuesto, se refiere a Peter Parker.
Con estas palabras que no pretenden ser más que un chiste, Marvel ha confirmado que E.D.I.T.H. sí recuerda a Peter Parker a pesar del hechizo de Strange. Parece que la magia no afecta a las IAs. Algo que podría ser muy interesante de cara al futuro, especialmente porque Peter se encuentra ahora casi sin recursos. Si puede acceder a su vieja asistente, las posibilidades que se le abrirían para actuar como héroe anónimo serían mucho mayores.
De qué va VisionQuest
"Visión, reiniciado y tras escapar de quienes buscaban utilizarlo como arma, ha permanecido oculto. En busca de un nuevo propósito, consulta las personalidades de inteligencia artificial integradas en su programación, entre ellas F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H., J.A.R.V.I.S. y el infame Ultrón. Su discreta existencia llega a su fin cuando una recompensa por su captura lo obliga a huir junto a Thomas Shepard, un misterioso joven que podría ser el hijo reencarnado de Visión", reza la sinopsis de VisionQuest.
"Mientras trata de evitar ser capturado, Visión deberá enfrentarse a su propia naturaleza, resistir la influencia de Ultrón y desentrañar el misterio que rodea a su joven compañero si quiere sobrevivir", concluye el fragmento compartido por Marvel. VisionQuest se estrena en Disney+ el 14 de octubre.

articles.title: Qualcomm launches two new smartphone chips with emphasis on AI | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Qualcomm today announced two flagship smartphone processors, called Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with a focus on facilitating better AI-focused features.
At its annual Snapdragon Summit, Qualcomm said that the new chips can aid in improved personalization for AI agents. The chips have new sensing hubs that can run small models of up to 200 million parameters. With the new sensing hub, smartphones can run a personal scribe locally and differentiate between speakers. Plus, it can build memory based on your usage for better suggestions for automating tasks. The company said that it can run a complete voice-in and voice-out agent through the new chip.
The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 has a new accelerator element that’s designed to run models in a more efficient way. The high-end Extreme version can run a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model locally. This means that while the overall model size is 30B, the model only activates a certain number of parameters for a particular task.
For comparison, at its Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) in June, Apple released a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, the most advanced of its third generation of foundation models.
The new Qualcomm CPU also provides pixel-level control for cameras to facilitate more pro-level experiences, along with improved stabilization and motion understanding. The Extreme version can support video recording at 8K 60fps and at 4K240 for ultra HD slow-motion. It also enables the new Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec for pro-level recording.
What’s more, both chips can use AI to boost vocals and reduce noise. Plus, it has Qualcomm’s new voice bubble tech, which isolates users’ noise during calls.
At the event, Motorola announced its Motorola Signature 27 smartphone, powered by the Snapdragon Gen 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with general availability sometime this year.
Qualcomm has been working on more than 40 AI devices, but there is still a belief that a lot of people will use their phones for AI rather than other dedicated devices. Nothing co-founder Carl Pei has hinted at this trend in the past, and more recently, new Apple CEO John Ternus reinforced the same line of thought during the iPhone Duo launch earlier this month.

articles.title: Multi-Agent AI Systems Must Work Like An Orchestra Without A Conductor
articles.text:
A mixture of expert agentic AI systems can focus on their tasks with or without a commanding general, but challenges remain in drawing boundaries between human and AI effort.
Key Takeaways:
Experts At The Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss recent developments and challenges when using agentic AI for chip design, with Matt Graham, senior group director of verification software product management at Cadence; Harrison Balistreri, head of business development and strategic partnerships at ChipAgents; Alexander Petr, senior director and portfolio manager at Keysight EDA; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at Siemens EDA; and Anand Thiruvengadam, executive director and head of AI product management at Synopsys. This roundtable was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. This is the third part of a three-part series. Part one is here. Part two is here.
L-R: Synopsys’ Thiruvengadam; Keysight’s Petr; Cadence’s Graham; ChipAgents’ Balistreri; and Siemens’ Balasubramanian.
SE: Many agentic flows involve a mixture of experts (MoE) or a hierarchy of multi-agents with some type of leader at the top. What developments are you seeing there? Is it a top-down, military-style organization with various security and access clearances, or more of a horizontal team?
Graham: It is becoming much flatter than an army. If you’d asked me a year ago, I might have said, yes, it is a big hierarchy of agents. There will be mini agents, sub agents, and low agents. There will be generals and lieutenants and whatever else, all the way up. But AI in general, not just EDA, we are migrating much more toward a flat set of skills, or capabilities, or features, or knowledge, or whatever the word is you want to use to describe it. Everything is overloaded with terms. What we’re seeing becomes a much more dynamic, task-based organization of skills into almost dynamic agents. There is one general, if you like, or commander.
Balasubramanian: Orchestrator.
Graham: Right. And everything else below tends to be much flatter. I can pick and choose quickly to assemble my troops, but it’s much less like an army with a mechanized division and an airborne division, or something else. We have troops. Those troops have skills, and we assemble the right troops for the task dynamically, because we’re not bound, as armies are, by logistical and physical reality.
Petr: You’re better off comparing it to an orchestra. You have one conductor, and you have groups who play certain instruments. They can play individually, or they can play together. They can also play synchronously or asynchronously to achieve certain tunes and then play together.
Balasubramanian: That’s very important. Even if it’s flat, the key thing is that everyone knows their part, and they also know how they connect to everyone else. Everyone knows the end goal. Nothing is siloed. They all play by the same tune. If you look at a symphony orchestra, everyone knows everyone else. They can read the notes. They know what to do, what not to do, how to do it.
Petr: There are borders, guardrails. They all ground it.
Balasubramanian: The term I see quite a bit is headless agents. There’s no concept of having a big master agent doing everything else. We call it a headless way of working, and it’s been quite popular on the software side. It’s coming here, and what I see going forward is customers are interacting with tools. They won’t even know what the tool is. From our side, we are going to build agentic capabilities coming out of the physical engines, or deterministic engines around those engines, and that’s going to be an agent on its own. It can talk to other agents. It can understand different formats and where it sits. It can talk to understand design. Designers can interact with it, make it do work. That’s where the future is going.
Thiruvengadam: What Matt said is very interesting. We are essentially making the point that you should be thinking about digital organization—human organization, human hierarchy, digital hierarchy, roughly speaking —which is correct. But also, the fluidity of that is very important. It won’t be a rigid, hard structure. Ebb and flow will happen. It can change, depending on the complexity of the commands. The fluidity is very important. You will have a layer that orchestrates and calls upon ‘resources’ as needed to execute. This is very important. At some point in the future, it might graduate to something where it’s maybe autonomous. That is about abstraction again. We are talking about taking layer after layer of abstraction away, one by one, but we’re not there yet.
Balistreri: We have products where agents propose hypotheses and do tournament-style ranking. We have a judging agent, but there’s a lot of nuance in this idea of agents, where you could throw many agents at the problem. But if they all come up with similar hypotheses for the problem, it doesn’t matter how many agents you deploy or how good your judging agent is. It has a lot to do with how you manage context, and it comes back to local versus global context. It doesn’t matter how you deploy agents if they all have the same local context. To get the benefit of deploying agents at scale, you need to manage which hypotheses each agent generates and where that context comes from. To do that, you also can’t have point agents. You can’t do point acceleration around one tool. Agents become powerful when they can deliver the full flow. The full flow requires encoding in your agent loops how to view some of this context and how to manage that, so that you get the benefit of many parallel agents instead of them just trying to converge on the same thing.
Graham: There are two sides to that, and I agree for the most part. But I’ll draw a parallel to how synthesis changed electronic design. The vast majority of gates built now are synthesized gates. The agent writes RTL. Then, RTL gets synthesized. But there is still a certain percentage, depending on the application, that must be either hand-synthesized or laid out by hand. There will still be significant opportunity to accelerate the tools. I wouldn’t call it a point agent necessarily. But in agentifying the tool for a specific task, a smaller percentage will still need to be hand-coded, in the same way that we still hand-assemble some instructions for a PC or for any compute platform. Expecting 100% autonomy is setting too high a bar that I don’t know we can achieve. I don’t think it’s realistic or even worthwhile. Setting it at 99-point-some-odd-nines still leaves a huge amount of work to be done, and accelerating the tools themselves is still important, but I agree that it’s not the bulk of the time.
Balistreri: This might be an unpopular opinion in this room, but we can talk about accelerating existing tools, or we can talk about new tools entirely. When we talk to our customers, one of the biggest bottlenecks in taping out their chips is that they don’t have enough on-premises compute to run existing EDA tools. Can you rearchitect tools to be optimized for agent use, speed up runtime, and run more tools in parallel? Then there’s the other question of, ‘Do the models subsume it?’ In some of the complex tasks that are still hand-placed, there is an opportunity for models to take that on and solve extremely complex problems that humans just couldn’t hold in their heads. Think about all those tables you had to look at on the wall. Back in the day, you were laying sheets across a giant table to look at the resistance and capacitance and placing them for analog. All of that, I think, can be captured inside of models.
Graham: It can be. The question is, how soon will it be efficient? We’ve spent a huge amount of time solving that problem deterministically, algorithmically, and mathematically so that we get the right answer every single time. What you’re proposing is, ‘Can we use a probabilistic model to solve those problems more efficiently?’ Today, ‘no’ is the very clear answer. With the speed of technological advancement, will that be compute-efficient and dollar-efficient in the next 2 years, 8 years, 10 years?
Thiruvengadam: I agree. The key point, again, is the march of nines. The march of nines will kick in, and you’ve got a 99.99999. You need to get 100% accuracy. We’re talking about subsuming two EDA tools into models.
Balasubramanian: That’s very important. In chip design, being 99.99% accurate is a failure. All it takes is one picosecond and you have a whole violation.
Petr: We keep forgetting that we still have not fully understood all the physics. Every single model we have is a simplification of the real world. It’s an error of an error of an error of an error. No matter how well you go on the whole agentic framework, at some point, there’s a trade-off somewhere. And if you don’t capture that, your chip is dead. We spent decades optimizing the simulator engines to get deterministic results. There’s always an argument in those AI frameworks, ‘Oh, just run reinforcement learning. It can do it.’ Fair, it can. But my mathematically based optimizer is still faster and more accurate. Why would I want to do that?
Thiruvengadam: It’s important to understand that the march of nines is a problem in software. Why would it not be a problem in hardware? In chip design, it’s even more of a problem. In software, they talk about getting 100%. Failure is an important part. In hardware, costs are so high that the march of nines becomes an even bigger problem.
Balasubramanian: As we go down the flow, the band of how much error you can tolerate drops drastically.
SE: In an orchestral multi-agentic flow, who has a kill switch to prevent agents from burning through tokens and trying forever to gain 100% coverage closure, for example?
Graham: This is part of the prep before you deploy, which must be part of the infrastructure. We all have infrastructure this must sit on — the guardrails. There are still infinite problems in IC design and verification. Fundamentally, it’s an infinite or near-infinite problem, so there must be guardrails somewhere on how much time, how many tokens, and what the tool covers, etc. One thing EDA has been good at over the years is having tool providers address that with customers, having customers understand the best ROI trade-offs, and pushing us to provide them. Up until now, it was cycles on a given problem. We get the number of CPU cycles we think we need to do, whether we get them in the cloud or on-prem or whatever, for one of the thousand tasks you have to do from RTL to GDS. Now we’re adding tokens to those, but we need the same guardrails. We know this. Our customers employ entire departments of people to optimize this exact problem.
Petr: Infinite loops are not new to us. Every mathematical problem has infinite loops. If you get into those trenches, we have solutions.
SE: What about IP ownership if you’re using an agent for a design that you sell to a customer, or they use your agent for their design, who owns what IP?
Balasubramanian: IP ownership is one of the biggest concerns I’m hearing about, both from our side as the tool provider and from the customer side. Yes, [agents] can write code, but the challenge is that all it takes is one copyrighted piece of code getting into your codebase, and if you don’t verify it, you’re going to get a loss. That’s one thing. Second, the most important thing is, I always tell people that any prompt you do, that’s your IQ. You’re doing your foundation, you’re using Claude Code, and you’re letting your designers do certain things. Their prompt will be, ‘This is how I’m going to be solving this routing problem. Can you do this?’ Your prompt is pretty much your IP. You’re telling some people the algorithm for how to do certain things, and there is a lot of talk about, ‘They’re not going to look at it.’ But every prompt is necessary to the LLM providers. If it goes outside of the air gap, it’s a problem. So IP protection is going to be very key. How do you expose code outside, especially source code? That’s going to be very key, and that’s a big concern coming up.
Petr: Another problem is that U.S. copyright does not allow us to copyright code that has been generated by an AI. That means every chip designed by an AI isn’t copyrightable.
Balasubramanian: Yes, because LLMs are not [copyrightable].
Thiruvengadam: The key distinction is that we are not talking about a chip that’s 100% designed by AI with no human intervention.
Petr: There’s a clause in the copyright that says the majority of the [design] has to be done by a human and, I’m sorry to say that, but the majority is not going to be.
Balistreri: I want to recap a bit and then get to this point. There are many problems, many layers of problems, with deploying AI in a high ROI way that organizations will accept meets their security requirements. One is cost. We solve that at the harness layer. The same model, doing like-for-like tasks, uses 40% fewer tokens. Our own model is open-weight and performs similarly, but at lower cost. Then there’s the full-flow problem, which is where you need the ontology. You can’t just do point acceleration. Then there’s the autonomous problem, which is the trust. Are there going to be critical errors? Are those gated and built into your system so you can’t produce things? Then there’s the IP and security issue, and it’s a pretty simple question. Do you want to send your inference over the public internet to a model provider that is building chips that compete with your chips? If you use frontier models in your agentic layer, whatever agents you use, you run that risk. Some don’t even have zero data retention. The clear answer to us — in a highly security-focused industry, where your design and design flow itself is IP — is that you need a solution with a custom model you can deploy on-prem. That also solves the IP question. I’m not a copyright lawyer, but if the design never leaves your environment, it’s de facto still yours. It’s not copyrighted per se, but no one else can access it.
Petr: Don’t underestimate reverse engineering.
Read parts one and two of the discussion:
Agentic AI Success Relies On Excellent Human Scaffolding
Before deploying agentic AI into a chip design, engineers must define the domain ontology and agentic harness. Fundamental engines are still crucial.
Token Costs Are Becoming The New EDA Budget Battle
Cost per token is causing EDA design budgets to balloon; what comes next isn’t entirely clear yet.

articles.title: Nigerian fintech startup Grey launches new payout routes to Senegal, Ivory Coast, Cameroon, Rwanda - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup Grey, the Y Combinator-backed cross-border payment platform, is now enabling direct payout to Senegal, Ivory Coast, Cameroon and Rwanda.
Grey enables individuals and businesses to easily own and manage multi-currency accounts in USD, GBP, and EUR, supporting transfers to more than 170 destinations. It also offers access to virtual cards.
With this new payout, migrants, diaspora communities, as well as individuals and businesses, can now send payments directly to recipients in these countries. Users can now send funds in the recipient’s local currency, including Rwandan francs (RWF), Central African CFA francs (XAF), and West African CFA francs (XOF).
Together, these four markets account for more than US$7 billion in remittance flows. Grey’s expansion is supporting these existing financial connections while making cross-border payments more accessible for the people and businesses that depend on them.
“Senegal, Ivory Coast, Cameroon and Rwanda have growing diasporas that send money home to support families, education, healthcare, and fund businesses. At the same time, people are travelling to Rwanda for vacations, to visit friends and relatives, for business and conferences. Yet cross-border payment has not always matched the strength of these relationships. With these new payouts, we’re making it easier for individuals and businesses to send money to these countries in their local currencies.” said Idorenyin Obong, CEO and co-founder of Grey.

articles.title: DataDome report finds bad bot traffic growing nine times faster than human traffic - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
DataDome report finds bad bot traffic growing nine times faster than human traffic
A new report out today from bot protection company DataDome SAS finds that malicious automated traffic grew 124% between July 2025 and June 2026, more than nine times the rate of human traffic growth — and most of the popular websites it tested could not stop a single bot.
The findings, from the 2026 edition of the company’s “State of Bot & Agent Security Report,” draw on more than a trillion requests across more than 75,000 customer sites, together with a June test of 21,491 popular websites. Scraping dominated the mix, at 70.9% of bad bot traffic and up 185.2% over the year. DataDome ties some of that growth to third-party data resellers and agent builders harvesting the web at scale for model training, activity that does not always identify itself as an artificial intelligence crawler.
Scalping, the use of bots to buy up limited inventory for resale, rose 290.7%, with median daily volume close to quadrupling, and fake account creation was up 34.5%. Distributed denial-of-service attacks grew 39.9% and peaked above 2 billion requests in a single day in April, which made them the second-largest category at 12.7% of bad bot traffic.
Credential stuffing was flat on the year. DataDome calls that pattern cyclical rather than fading, since volume surged through the summer of 2025, collapsed by nearly 90% and then reached new single-day highs by April.
AI traffic grew 82.3% over the same 12 months. DataDome logged 52.7 billion AI agent and crawler requests across its customer base, with Meta-affiliated bots generating 46.3% of the identified total and OpenAI-affiliated bots 34.6%. Of the 29.02 billion AI bot requests logged in the first half of 2026, 97.9% still went to homepages and other general content.
The other 2.1% is where the change shows up. AI agents sent 605.6 million requests to login, form, cart, payment and account-creation pages between January and June, and login pages took 51.7% of that, against 23% a year earlier. Monthly login-page volume from AI bots ran from 11.9 million requests in January to 99.7 million in June.
Jerome Segura, vice president of threat research at DataDome, said automated traffic is “growing fast” and moving into the login, account and transaction flows at the center of the customer journey. Identifying automation is not the hard part anymore, he said. The harder question is whether a given session is beneficial or harmful.
DataDome’s website test ran in June, sending 10 bot types at 21,491 sites across 15 industries from residential addresses in the U.S., Canada and France. Nearly two in three sites, 65.3%, stopped none of them, and the share reaching full protection has fallen two years running, to 2.4% from 8.4% in 2024, though this year’s test added harder bot types. Telecommunications sites were the weakest, at 82.9% unprotected.
Spoofed AI agents walked past more than seven sites in 10. DataDome calls identity-based trust a widespread weakness, since a request claiming to be GPTBot, ClaudeBot or another trusted crawler is often let through on the name alone. Only 5.5% of sites caught the test’s disguised bot, which forges the network fingerprint of a real browser.
Most of the defenses in use are “still largely built around binary choices,” Segura said, even as the calls organizations have to make get finer. The critical test, in his view, is whether a site can separate a legitimate AI assistant from a credential-testing bot or an account-abuse campaign. Blocking everything would also cut off beneficial activity, he added.
